summary: Describes a TCP extension, the MD5 signature option, to enhance security for BGP sessions by authenticating each segment. It was replaced by RFC 5925.

eli5.summary: A secret stamp on every message between two routers to prove it really came from the other one.

questions: what is the tcp md5 signature option
how does tcp md5 protect bgp
subtitle: A signature stamped on every TCP segment so a BGP router can ignore forged packets, especially forged resets.

tldr.problem: BGP runs over TCP, so an attacker who injects forged TCP segments, especially resets, can disrupt a routing session.
tldr.mechanism: A new TCP option carries a 16-byte MD5 digest computed over the pseudo-header, the TCP header, the data and a secret key known to both ends. A segment whose digest does not match is silently dropped.
tldr.outcome: It was a weak but widely practiced protection, and the RFC itself warns that MD5 is no longer considered strong. It has been obsoleted by RFC 5925.

today: RFC 2385 is obsoleted by RFC 5925 and was updated by RFC 6691. The RFC itself describes its protection as weak and as current practice rather than a lasting answer.

sections.title: Why BGP Needs Protection
sections.content:
The main goal is to let BGP protect itself against spoofed TCP segments being slipped into its connection. The RFC is most worried about forged TCP resets.

To spoof a protected connection, an attacker would have to guess the TCP sequence numbers and also know the password that is mixed into the digest. That password never appears in the connection itself. There is no negotiation: whether a connection uses the option is purely a matter of site policy.

An IESG note says the document describes existing practice for securing BGP against certain simple attacks, and that it is understood to have security weaknesses against concerted attacks.
sections.eli5: Imagine two friends passing notes in class. A stranger could slip in a fake note, so the friends agree on a secret mark that only they know.

sections.title: How the Signature Is Computed
sections.content:
Every segment sent on a protected connection carries a 16-byte MD5 digest. The digest is computed over these items, in order:

  1. the TCP pseudo-header (source IP address, destination IP address, zero-padded protocol number and segment length)
  2. the TCP header, excluding options, with the checksum taken as zero
  3. the segment data, if any
  4. a key or password known to both TCPs

The nature of the key is deliberately left unspecified. The receiver computes its own digest from the same data with its own key and compares. A failing comparison must make it drop the segment and must not produce any response. Logging the failure is probably advisable.

Unlike options such as Window Scale, the absence of this option in the SYN,ACK must not make the sender stop signing. Signing is under the complete control of the application, not of whether the remote host understands the option.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix the message with the secret and write down the result. If the receiver mixes the same way and gets a different result, it ignores the message without saying anything.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content: The option has Kind 19 and Length 18, followed by the MD5 digest. The digest is always 16 bytes long, and the option appears in every segment of a protected connection.
sections.eli5: It is a small labeled box at the front of each message. The label says what the box is, and the box holds the stamp.

sections.title: Side Effects and Costs
sections.content:
A connectionless reset is ignored by the receiver, because whoever sent it does not know the key. So a connection attempt to a port with no listener times out instead of being refused, and resets for stale connections are ignored too. The RFC notes this can be a problem operationally, since resets help BGP recover quickly from peer crashes.

Signing costs time. In one sample implementation on a 100 MHz R4600, a signature for a simple ACK took an average of 0.0268 ms and one for a data segment carrying 4096 bytes took 0.8776 ms. These costs apply on both the input and output paths.

The option also uses header space. The MSS offered must account for at least 18 more bytes of header, and the TCP header may be at most 60 bytes, leaving 40 bytes for options. The RFC works through a 4.4BSD SYN whose options total exactly 40 bytes with the digest included.

Implementations should support at minimum a key of printable ASCII of 80 bytes or less.
sections.eli5: The stamp makes every message a bit bigger and takes a little time to make. It also means fake "hang up" notes are ignored, which is good, but real ones from a confused peer are ignored too.

sections.title: The Weakness of MD5
sections.content:
The RFC says the mechanism is weak but currently practiced, and that stronger mechanisms are anticipated in future work. Since the memo was first issued, MD5 has been found vulnerable to collision search attacks and is considered by some to be insufficiently strong for this use.

It still specifies MD5 because the option was already deployed operationally and no algorithm type field existed to allow an upgrade under the same option number. Another similar option using a different hash such as SHA-1 is not prevented, but that would need another document.
sections.eli5: The secret stamp is a bit old-fashioned and clever attackers have found tricks against it. The authors say so and expect something better later.

references.text: Rivest, R., "The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm," RFC 1321, April 1992.
